E046-01.notes: A is a comma splice ('a kit, it contained'). B 'a kit, and contained' makes Robbins the subject of 'contained', which is illogical. D 'a kit contained a board' leaves two finite verbs with no connector, so it is ungrammatical. C uses a restrictive relative clause and reads cleanly.

E046-02.notes: Not knowing where to display the kits is the cause of the poor sales, so 'because' fits. B 'although' sets up a contrast that isn't there. C 'so' reverses cause and effect. D 'unless' gives an illogical condition. The comma before 'because' is acceptable.

E046-03.notes: Redundancy item. B 'improved and got better', C 'dramatically ... in a dramatic way' and D 'dramatically and greatly' each repeat the same idea. A is concise.

E046-04.notes: The phrase gives the brand name (Craft Master), which the essay states nowhere else. A is wrong because the phrase gives no cause for the sales rise. C is wrong because the name is not repeated anywhere. D is wrong because the phrase does not contradict sentence 5, which was about the early kits. The fact checks out: Palmer sold the kits as Craft Master.

E046-05.notes: After an independent clause, a colon correctly introduces the explanatory phrase. A uses a semicolon before a fragment. B puts the fragment after a period. C puts 'and' after the colon, which makes the construction ungrammatical.

E046-06.notes: Sentence 10 gives the critics' reason: a picture that came with instructions isn't art. A is wrong because there is no sales or magazine evidence. B is wrong because that view belongs to the critics, not Robbins. D is wrong because the sentence says nothing about instructions printed on the board.

E046-07.notes: The subject is 'the kits' (plural); the 'along with' phrase does not change the number. 'Were' also keeps the past tense of the reported argument. A 'was', C 'is' and D 'has been' are all singular, and C and D also shift tense.

E046-08.notes: 'Today' calls for the present tense. A 'were' and B 'had been' are past tenses, and C 'will have been' is future perfect, so none fits.

E046-09.notes: The order is Klein's initial doubt, then poor early sales, then the improvement after the demonstration, then the later success. That order is already logical. B and C would put 'early kits sold poorly' after the success. D would put the sales result before the owner's initial doubt, which is weaker; 'Early kits' also sits naturally right before the 'Sales improved' contrast in 6.

E046-10.notes: The antecedent is 'Americans' (plural), so the plural possessive 'their' is needed. A 'its' is singular. B 'there' is an adverb. D 'they're' is a contraction for 'they are'.

E046-11.notes: Dangling modifier: whatever was 'Baked in a Bundt pan' has to be the cake. A puts 'a ring of soft fudge' there, B puts Helfrich there, and C puts the expletive 'there'; all three are wrong. D makes the cake the subject. The facts are accurate: 1966 Pillsbury Bake-Off, Ella Helfrich of Texas, second place, Tunnel of Fudge.
